title: A Debate: Is University Worth the Investment?

dialogue.speaker: Moderator
dialogue.text: Today's debate: "University is no longer worth the investment for most students." For the motion: Baglan. Against: Aliya.

dialogue.speaker: Baglan
dialogue.text: I'll be direct. The world has been changing faster than universities have been adapting. While institutions have been maintaining the same four-year degree structure for decades, the job market has been demanding different skills — coding, data literacy, entrepreneurship. Students who have been spending four years and significant money for credentials are increasingly finding those credentials don't guarantee employment. Furthermore, online learning has been improving dramatically. You can now study from MIT or Cambridge for free. So why pay?

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: Baglan makes a point I've been expecting. But it misses something important. Yes, online learning has been expanding. Yes, the job market has been changing. But university has never only been about credentials. It has been providing something that no online course has replicated: sustained intellectual community. You spend years in rooms with people who are challenging what you believe. That has been producing something that no syllabus measures.

dialogue.speaker: Baglan
dialogue.text: But that community has been becoming less affordable for more people. While we've been debating its value, the cost has been rising. Students have been taking on significant debt before they've earned a single tenge professionally. That debt has been shaping their choices in ways they wouldn't have chosen freely.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: I agree the cost issue is serious. But the solution isn't to abandon university — it's to fund it better. Countries that have been investing in higher education as a public good have been producing more innovation, more social mobility, and more civic engagement. The correlation has been documented across decades. The question isn't whether university creates value. It's who is paying for that value, and whether the distribution is fair.

dialogue.speaker: Baglan
dialogue.text: Even accepting that, has the university experience been keeping pace with reality? Most programmes have been teaching the same content they've been teaching for twenty years. The world has been moving on. I've been talking to employers who have been saying for years that graduates are arriving without the skills they need.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: Those employers have also been hiring graduates consistently. Actions speak more clearly than complaints. Moreover, the skills gap they've been describing — communication, critical thinking — are skills universities have always been developing. Not always through lectures, but through the whole experience of being there.

dialogue.speaker: Moderator
dialogue.text: A sharp debate. You've been giving us a lot to think about. Let's open it to the floor.
